article.title: Who is Against Mass Struggle?
article.content: Claire Wright and Sarah Milner respond to Socialist Majority on the “democratic road to socialism” and DSA’s endorsement process. Signed articles do not necessarily represent the collective views of Reform & Revolution. In August, comrades in Socialist Majority Caucus published an article titled “Why We Endorse: The Case for Nithya Raman,” a supportive piece of DSA-LA’s endorsement of Raman. Raman has become something of a lightning rod for criticism in DSA owing to the relatively large gap between her perceived association with DSA (which is very high) versus her adherence to the principles of DSA and her commitment to DSA’s program (which, even by the standards of elected officials, is quite low, such as her refusal to part with her self-identification as a capitalist). This separation led to Groundwork, a caucus typically aligned with SMC, to oppose Raman’s endorsement in the LA primary. Since the Springs of Resolution resolution in early November to expel and unendorse Nithya Raman ultimately failed, our caucus has drawn severe criticism for voting against it. As such, we have been portrayed as supporters of Raman’s endorsement. In reality, it was our belief that it was naive to try to force LA to overturn their endorsement, through extraordinary measures such as revoking dues share from the chapter and even attacking them through lawsuits in the bourgeois courts. Lost in this, however, has been the vital point — this endorsement was a catastrophic mistake by the chapter. They should have voted Raman down. It is incredibly clear that the debate over Raman isn’t just about Raman, nor just about Los Angeles. It is merely the latest beachhead of a long debate about how DSA should relate to its electeds. Hence, we may use this current debate to reflect on how our strategies and tactics differ within DSA on this question and continue with clarity. SMC proposes three points for understanding endorsements in their article: 1. We endorse candidates to move forward on the democratic road to socialism . 2. DSA’s endorsements are not statements of our values but vehicles for our power. 3. Engaging in mass struggle makes us stronger, abstentionism makes us weaker. At first blush, these positions are a sharp and pointed framework for DSA’s electoral program. These positions also demonstrate the marked difference between SMC’s politics and comrades who desire a higher endorsement standard. In fact, these are framed intentionally to draw a dividing line between themselves and their supporters, framed as reasonable pragmatists, and the DSA left, who they would deride as “ultras”. In the latter two points, SMC have not actually outlined the difference in strategy between caucuses; in fact, with limited nuances, they have described ideas with which almost any caucus could find alignment. They have set up truisms which would be ludicrous to disagree with and then have inaccurately presented these truisms as the dividing lines in DSA. Hence, these final two points are of limited utility for navigating electoral disagreements. There are very few electoral abstentionists left in DSA’s electoral project with any significant influence. The vast majority of members not only support engaging in electoral work and making endorsements, but in fact agree, with varying degrees of subtlety, with the premise that endorsements are as much a tactic as a statement of principles. Consider: There is no candidate among our congressional slate or other prominent elected officials who clearly reflects DSA’s full positions and program. Is any candidate aggressively campaigning on abolition, Jerusalem as the capital of Palestine, and so forth? Has Zohran agitated to abolish the Senate? Assuredly not, yet the leftward cadre of NYC-DSA fought for his election all the same. Beyond that question, consider: most of the DSA “left” voted for a program more radical than “Workers Deserve More”—yet none of us have set that higher bar as the exclusive endorsement threshold. Every caucus endorses candidates they disagree with, and even that the majority of DSA members might disagree with. Almost everyone in DSA knows that candidates with politics worse than the average active DSA leader can still grow the movement. They may not conceptualize these endorsements as tactical but they still, sometimes, support them. “Building the power of the movement” is not actually a certain, objective measure. One can frame this pragmatism with the idea of taking one step back to take two steps forward. Not a worthless perspective by any means. Yet, not every “pragmatic” demand is necessarily the right decision. Take, for example, Zohran’s recent courting of Zionist groups through his Anti-Semitism Task Force. This was billed as a pragmatic decision to reduce opposition to his affordability agenda. A solid logic! Yet, it became clear (and was clear prior) that the Zionist lobby in New York City would hardly be swayed by his overtures. Zohran made one stride back to inch forward, and found himself behind. In electoral debates this can be seen through the “Warren Question”. Would you endorse Elizabeth Warren for senate? Objectively , she is one of the most left wing members of Congress. Objectively , she has played an important role in shifting American politics leftward. Yet, few if any DSA members would openly call for her endorsement. She’s already in office, her winning does little to build the movement, etc. What really separates Warren from Nithya Raman? If LA endorses Nithya to push the needle leftward, why do we not endorse somebody like Warren? Why do we not endorse Abdul El-Sayed or Brad Lander? And so on. Yet just as it becomes clear even the so-called “ultra” wing can compromise, even DSA’s supposedly pragmatic, “against red lines” wing, you will find, has lines. Dig far enough, and you will find that, just as everyone has a point where the gains of a campaign outweigh the problems of a candidate, each and every caucus has a moment where the problems of a candidate outweigh their benefits, where the steps in either direction combine to move too far backwards. Coming to the latter conclusion about any particular race does not an abstentionist make. So what exactly is happening with electoral work? The issue is that we are trying to communicate our beliefs through a tremendous mess of contradictory incentives, interests and messages. Electoral organizing, filtered through the disorienting and chaotic landscape of the capitalist media, with certain points coming through clearly and some very messily, is the terrain we are forced to struggle on. Though many don’t want to admit it, we all agree: There aren’t many candidates who actually share our full DSA politics right now. A better way to navigate this dispute is to drill into the details of what message, exactly, a particular endorsement will convey. In the case of Raman, her failures on Palestine and tepid stance on representing DSA’s program will be the things that cut through the static to the general populace. We did not send the message we wish to through LA’s endorsement. It was an opportunist failure and a mistake. Each caucus would do well to articulate where they draw the line and what factors they consider to be most crucial in determining whether a candidate or campaign’s potential may outpace its political weaknesses or contradictions. A debate on these terms would be much more fruitful. The vast majority of our endorsed candidates are not caucused, cadre members with specific, factionally developed internal positions on how DSA should organize. This leaves all factions, but most often those on the left of DSA, in a reactive, passive role, advancing our politics through critique and response rather than through setting the example. There are exceptions to this to be sure, and the tremendous growth of our organization and blossoming of many 2026 campaigns has begun to turn the tide. But we still have more work ahead of us. Running many caucus members and close allies across DSA’s political spectrum, who can either prove theories in practice, or fail in such a way we are forced to reevaluate, is a critical next step for our political development, and as an extension the socialist project. So fighting abstention as a principle is boxing with shadows. Does that mean the difference between DSA caucuses is merely a matter of degrees, a matter of where a line is drawn? Not exactly. Principles 2 and 3 from SMC create a binary between “Statements & Abstentionism” versus “Action & Mass Struggle,” an absurdity which is intended to muddle the discussion, as no self-respecting socialist outside of the sects which have plagued the American left would find themselves in the latter. That being said — the argument here is not that the differences between DSA’s caucuses on the question of electeds is merely one of tactics. Rather, while we in actuality all exist on the “mass struggle” side of SMC’s binary, that side still has groups with fundamentally different foundations and theories of change. The Democratic Road to Socialism DSA’s new program, “Workers Deserve More,” sets out some conceptions of what we envision as the horizon of our project. It includes lines like “building a party whose goal is a democratic socialism of the working class” and “we know complete victory will require building a new society from the ground up.” These are contentions with which most DSA members would agree. However, when it comes to the specific form that the transformation of society will take, Workers Deserve More leaves the question open. How do we build a new society? What does the transition between this society and that one look like? Within the latter two principles outlined by SMC, there lay more or less two approaches, and their first principle clarifies with which their strategy lies: T he Democratic Road to Socialism. Contrary, perhaps, to its name, the “democratic road to socialism” is not a general Democratic Socialist answer to these questions; rather, it is a specific factional contention which some democratic socialists subscribe to. Rooted in the works of Ralph Miliband and Nicos Poulantzas and developed by many successive generations of socialist organizers, it posits that the contradictions of the capitalist state can be exploited by a surging mass movement of socialists and workers transforming the state from both the inside and the outside, which requires elected officials of the socialist party to take the reins of the bourgeois state. Understanding this framework, one can see where talk of capturing the state and plans for a Project 2029 from publications like Geese, who are aligned with this theory of change, originates. Let us not mince words. We, the authors, are Bolshevists and we are Revolutionists. We do not eschew the electoral realm of struggle, just as those revolutionaries past such as Lenin and Luxemburg did not. Our fundamental demarcation from the “democratic road” as it exists in DSA is twofold. Firstly, we reject what is essentially a modernization of Menshevik two-stage theory. To quote from Groundwork’s Thought Library: “Communists and Socialists must complete the work of reconstruction…and allow a new contradiction (!) between the multiracial bourgeoisie and the multiracial proletariat to become the driving force in the politics of the United States” Herein, the argument is that white supremacy must first be overcome before the socialist transformation of society can be accomplished. To this end, we must shy away from an independent class position to build a broad, “progressive” alliance with liberalism. We reject this entirely. Because racial oppression is the bedrock of capitalism in the U.S., Reconstruction can only be completed through socialist revolution. Our second demarcation, then, is with what is essentially the ultimate blow against the bourgeois order — we know that we cannot use the existing state machinery as a cudgel of emancipation, and as such we do not see the election of socialists to office as a form of “taking state power.” Therefore, what we seek from our electeds is, to quote Lenin, for them to be: …tribune[s] of the people , who is able to react to every manifestation of tyranny and oppression, … who is able to generalize all these manifestations and produce a single picture of police violence and capitalist exploitation; who is able to take advantage of every event, however small, in order to set forth before all [their] socialist convictions and [their] democratic demands, in order to clarify for all and everyone the world-historic significance of the struggle for the emancipation of the proletariat. “But wait!”, the Democratic Roader cries, “could you not make that argument for all of our electeds? Are you not just making a fake bar so you can condemn all of our electeds?” Not so! For a recent and shining example, let us present Darializa Avila Chevalier. She has not so much as entered Congress yet, but following the shooting of a local man by ICE, she was found going door-to-door informing the people of their rights, loudly agitating for our program and to abolish ICE proudly under the flag of the Democratic Socialists, and even taking blows from the police! That is not to say that Darializa is perfect, nor that all of our other electeds are irredeemable opportunists. It is to point out that it is entirely possible for such isolated tribune-like actions to instead become the norm. The standard. However, this sort of action is a rare thing for DSA’s Socialists in Office. Reform & Revolution owes its name chiefly to Luxemburg’s famous pamphlet, but we owe our philosophy of class struggle to Trotsky’s conception of the transitional method. If abstain from day-to-day struggle in the name of revolutionary purity, then we are an unserious and untested clique of propagandists. If we limit our political horizon solely to reform struggles, however, then we reduce ourselves to policy advisers for the ruling class. We fight to build, advance, and link together all the struggles of the workers and oppressed in order to link the felt needs of our class to the need for socialist revolution. The role of a Socialist In Office, like the Militant-led Liverpool City Council in the 1980s, is to fight unambiguously for our movement and for the working class. As we send the biggest slate of socialists to congress in American history this January, it would do us well to ponder on what those demands may be, and how our electeds can champion them. This brings us back to Raman. Considering her record, when those “manifestations of tyranny and oppression” come, will she side decisively with the people? Or will she tidily administer the bourgeois order, as she has said she would? We may debate this point, but let us have no illusions about where the battle lines are drawn. We do not denounce the use of Raman as a progressive ally, we do not denounce support for her administration — but we do not believe she is a tribune of the people nor a champion of the socialist movement, and we believe this is what an endorsement should merit. The question is not “shall we engage in mass struggle?” The question is “who should our champions be?”
